headlines.title: Vallejo homeowner considers legal action against PG&E after tree removal leaves massive log pile
headlines.description: A Vallejo homeowner is considering legal action against Pacific Gas and Electric Co. after utility crews removed a large tree from her backyard in June but left behind a massive pile of heavy logs. Catherine, a Vallejo resident, said she understood why the tree needed to come down because it was overgrown and leaning dangerously close to power lines. “The tree was overgrown and close to the lines so it was going sideways so it was better to remove it,” Catherine said. However, crews left behind a pile of large logs that she says she cannot move on her own, creating an obstacle and a potential safety hazard. “Well I can not walk…blocks my way around the property, and it’s close to my house…this is flammable material,” Catherine said. According to PG&E’s online policy regarding tree safety work, branches under 4 inches thick are generally chipped or removed, while larger wood is left on the property for the homeowner to manage. Even so, Catherine maintains that a PG&E inspector verbally promised that someone would return to haul the logs away or cut them into pieces so she could dispose of them herself. She could not provide written documentation of the agreement. “Those are absolutely unspeakable,” Catherine said. “That it’s left to myself, an elderly lady to handle, there’s no way I can handle it.” Describing the situation as an unfulfilled promise, Catherine expressed deep frustration. “On one hand PG&E doing a good job cleaning the trees but on the other hand they’re leaving behind huge debris for people to do what?” she asked. “This is vandalism and my property it’s intentional…elderly abuse….infliction of emotional distress,” Catherine added. PG&E officials stated that the utility is looking into the matter. In a statement, the company said: “We’re taking this seriously and are now reviewing our records to get a better understanding of what work we were doing at this customer’s address. We expect to have those details tomorrow.” Catherine said that if the issue is not resolved this week, she plans to move forward with legal action.

headlines.title: San Francisco faces deadline to submit bid to buy PG&E assets
headlines.description: Tuesday is the deadline for San Francisco to submit an official bid to state regulators if the city wants to operate its own power company. San Francisco is offering $3.4 billion to buy PG&E’s assets, but NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit has learned PG&E will counter with a price of at least $20 billion. In its offer, San Francisco is not including what city officials said are costs the city will bear on its own, such as creating a new station to handle getting power and delivering it to the grid. PG&E includes those larger costs. San Francisco said it has recorded 40 power outages so far this year. City leaders continue to ask state regulators to get to the bottom of what they call the utility’s reliability issues. San Francisco Apr 21 San Francisco Mar 31 PG&E disagrees. Last week, CEO Patti Poppe told the Climate One group that PG&E actually has less outage time this year. Poppe also said San Francisco is vastly underestimating the cost of taking over the utility and undervaluing its assets. “I imagine there will be a convoy of blue and white trucks driving across the Bay Bridge to Oakland, never to come back,” Poppe said. “I don’t think that’s in San Francisco’s best interest. And we’ll fight about that.” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu said the city will likely rehire many of those workers. Chiu called Poppe’s talk of a $20 billion value “absurdly inflated,” citing the city suffering one major outage a week on average. The California Public Utilities Commission is in the process of determining a fair and just value for a potential sale. That process will take time, and the issue could also end up in court.

headlines.title: Proposal to turn abandoned SF Centre mall into data center and AI lab faces pushback from Mayor Lurie
headlines.description: The abandoned San Francisco Centre mall could find new life as a massive data center and artificial intelligence lab under a newly revealed proposal, though the idea faces immediate hurdles from city leadership and community members. The multistory shopping mall has been closed and boarded up since late January. According to a proposal confirmed by Jared Kreiger, CEO of the Maryland-based property development firm KG Growth Partners, a confidential client is exploring purchasing the entire property to convert the upper floors into a data center and AI lab. The plan would include public space on the ground level and water for a rooftop community garden that could be donated to nonprofits focusing on food insecurity. However, Kreiger declined to reveal the identity of the prospective buyer. The proposal comes at a complicated time for downtown San Francisco. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie approved a 45-day moratorium on City Hall approving any permits to build new data centers in the city. Addressing the proposal, Mayor Lurie said he was unaware of the plan and emphasized that the building remains on the market. “I am not aware of that proposal,” Lurie said. “The building is still up for sale. There is not a buyer yet. I’m hopeful that we get someone in there that will bring a lot of people downtown.” Communities across the country have increasingly raised concerns over data center developments, pointing to issues such as heavy water usage, environmental impacts, round-the-clock noise, and vibrations. Local reactions to the downtown San Francisco concept were mixed. “I’ve heard bad things about data centers,” said San Francisco resident Paul Bodner. “By default I would not support it,” added Guillaume Le Ster, also of San Francisco. Nicholas McNely, who lives a couple of blocks from the shuttered mall, questioned the motives behind such a project. “They’re more trying to extract from whatever community they’re trying to extract the resources from to enrich themselves so, I don’t really see the reason for a data center here,” McNely said. Conversely, some visitors saw potential upside. Janet Li of Burlingame noted, “If it’s an AI center here, more people would work here so, I think it’s good for the street.” The proposal was first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and confirmed to NBC Bay Area by development consultants.

headlines.title: Federal grant cuts threaten South Bay housing program for 40 vulnerable patients
headlines.description: A South Bay community clinic is scrambling to secure alternative funding after federal grant cuts slashed more than $400,000 from a vital housing program, leaving 40 vulnerable patients at risk of losing their homes. Bay Area Community Health, which operates clinics from Hayward to Gilroy, recently learned that its annual funding for the Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS program has dried up. Dr. Zettie Page, president and CEO of BACH, said the clinic only found out about the cuts a week ago. Noting that the health centers primarily serve uninsured, underinsured, and special populations cycling in and out of employment, Page emphasized that stable housing is a vital pillar of health care. “Because our health centers really focus on uninsured and underinsured, and those who have neither, we really work to target those in special populations, and those who are in and out of employment,” Page said. “We just became aware of this a week ago,” Page added. “So the what now is still on the table.” The sudden funding cliff forced BACH to notify the 40 affected families that their housing subsidies will end on Oct. 30 — less than two weeks away. NBC Bay Area reporter Damian Trujillo noted that because these individuals are already in highly vulnerable situations, there are deep concerns they could end up on the streets. San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan placed the blame squarely on federal decisions, sharply criticizing the cuts. “Forty vulnerable people potentially right out on the streets,” Mahan said. “Medically vulnerable. They cannot work. They have life-altering medical conditions.” “We need to shine a spotlight on the cruelty of the Trump administration’s policies,” Mahan added. “These are health care and housing cuts that are targeting the most vulnerable people.” Mahan stated that the city cannot afford to backfill the $400,000 due to its own ongoing budget shortfalls. Instead, city leaders are actively engaging with the South Bay congressional delegation and hoping the county will release Measure A funds intended for emergencies of this scale. “I think it’s irresponsible,” Mahan said. “I think it’s cruel, and this is what these policies look like in practice.” NBC Bay Area reached out to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for comment but has not yet received a response. Meanwhile, BACH staff remain devastated, worried that the impacted families face severe uncertainty heading into the cold winter months and the holidays.

headlines.title: Growing beaver population could impact salmon along San Jose's Guadalupe River
headlines.description: A growing beaver population in the South Bay may become a problem for efforts to increase salmon in the area. The South Bay Clean Creeks Coalition is keeping a hopeful eye on the Guadalupe River in San Jose, where beavers are making themselves at home and working to build dams. The dams are starting to partially block waterways at a time when local salmon are ready to spwan. Beaver dams can help spawning salmon because they aid in the creation of wetlands and provide shelter for baby salmon. But excessive silt caused by the dams can create issues in areas where the salmon lay their eggs. The coalition is asking the Santa Clara Valley Water District to try to find a solution that allows both the salmon and beavers to coexist.

headlines.title: Suspected DUI driver arrested after 2 killed in wrong-way crash on I-680 in Concord
headlines.description: A woman was arrested Monday on suspicion of driving under the influence following a wrong-way crash on Interstate 680 in Concord that left two people dead, according to the California Highway Patrol. The head-on collision happened at about 1:50 a.m. on northbound Interstate 680, just south of Willow Pass Road, the CHP said. Citing a preliminary investigation, the CHP said a black Lexus sedan – driven by a woman and carrying three passengers – was heading south in the northbound lanes of I-680 when it slammed into a black Chevrolet sedan driven by a woman. Two passengers in the Lexus died at the scene, according to the CHP. The third Lexus passenger and both drivers suffered major injuries. The Lexus driver was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence, the CHP said. Two of the passengers in the Lexus, including one who died, were not wearing seatbelts at the time of the collision, according to the CHP. Everyone else was wearing their seatbelt. An investigation into the crash is underway.

headlines.title: Monday is the last day to register online to vote in Nov. 3 election
headlines.description: If you aren’t already registered to vote, state officials are reminding residents that Monday is the last day to register online to cast a ballot in the upcoming Nov. 3 General Election. Eligible Californians can register or update their voter registration online through midnight Monday, at registertovote.ca.gov. “The website is mobile-friendly and allows people to register or update their voter registration on a laptop, tablet, or smartphone,” said California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber. Voters who are unsure about their status can check it at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov. Eligible voters who miss Monday’s online registration deadline have the option of “Same Day” or “Conditional” voter registration, but they must do so in person at their county elections office or at any in-person voting location through Election Day. Those voters will be asked to fill out a voter registration form and will be provided a ballot, which will only be counted after the county elections office has completed the voter registration verification process, state officials said. More information is available at caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2

headlines.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say
headlines.description: A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings. Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention. “Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources — including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.” A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov. 6. Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship. Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said. Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond. “Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033. Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond. After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment. Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son. But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked. Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia. Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest. Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30. Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.” OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence. __ Marcelo reported from New York.
headlines.source: Barbara Ortutay and Philip Marcelo | The Associated Press

headlines.title: San Jose officer hurt during traffic stop that prompted police shooting
headlines.description: A San Jose police officer was injured during a traffic stop that prompted another officer to shoot their gun, authorities said. The incident was reported 2:54 a.m. Monday when police stopped a vehicle in the area of North 21st and Santa Clara streets. San Jose police said the traffic stop “led to an officer getting injured and a second officer discharging a firearm.” The suspect vehicle then sped off. Police said a possible suspect vehicle was found in the area of Lucretia Avenue and Tully Road. The officer’s injuries are considered non-life threatening, police said. headlines.title: Justice Department carries out California sweep targeting alleged noncitizen voters
headlines.description: Federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered and voted in U.S. elections. The arrests are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month’s midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. They also reflect a further escalation in a simmering voter roll fight between the federal government and California that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued the state and later warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution. The Justice Department said the 28 people who were charged as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations. “This causes real damage to real elections and real damage to American citizens,” Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department, said during a news conference in Los Angeles to announce the charges. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. While some states voluntarily handed over the information, the department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain it — lawsuits that so far have been unsuccessful. The Justice Department said Monday it has charged 113 people in 20 states with illegal voting and illegal registration offenses over the last several weeks, It earlier said it had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. The operation Monday involved the four U.S. attorneys’ offices across California in what the Justice Department intended as a statewide show of force. Among the dozens of people arrested was a 72-year-old Belize-born man who is accused of voting illegally in four elections. Dozens of federal agents descended on the man’s residential cul-de-sac in Commerce, a small city in Los Angeles County, to make the arrest. The man was put in handcuffs in his pajamas and taken into federal custody downtown. Others emerged from the house to watch and questioned the number of heavily armed officers present for the arrest, as well as the need for handcuffs. The arrests were the latest in a flurry of activity that has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Over 23 million people are registered statewide. The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. McCotter said the 20,000 number was likely to rise. “That’s just the floor,” he said. As part of its lawsuit, the Justice Department filed paperwork Monday seeking a court order that would force California to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens and to independently, or in conjunction with the federal government, verify their citizenship status before tabulating their mail-in ballot. The Justice Department asked for the order to be entered in time for the Nov. 3 election. Absent that order, the government said, “there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted.” Requests for comment sent Monday to the secretary of state, state attorney general and governor’s office were not immediately returned. Attorney General Rob Bonta ‘not impressed’ by federal case California Attorney General Rob Bonta was asked about the arrests during a news conference in San Francisco focused on the state’s efforts to combat cryptocurrency scams. Bonta said that while voter fraud is serious, the number of arrests announced Monday represents roughly .0001% of the state’s more than 23 million registered voters and that the arrests aren’t evidence of widespread voter fraud, even if the allegations turn out to be true. “I think the announcement today by the United States DOJ makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud, but when there are isolated incidents, one-off incidents of voter fraud, those are wrong, those are illegal, and those individuals should be held accountable,” Bonta said. Bonta also said the DOJ’s list of “likely noncitizens” doesn’t include any evidence to support the federal government’s suspicions. “They’re not saying that we have visible proof. They’re not even saying that we know,” Bonta said. “They’re not even saying we think we have. They’re saying we believe it’s likely.” He said the last time federal prosecutors made a similar claim was when they thought there were 16,000 ineligible voters in Nevada but were unable to substantiate a single case of voter fraud. “We are not impressed by their case. We are not impressed by their position,” Bonta said. “We believe their case is meritless and will make our position very clear in court.” A warning for poll workers On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a letter warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation. “The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from McCotter. It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.” The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. “The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said. ___ Bay City News and Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report.
headlines.source: Safiyah Riddle | The Associated Press and Thom Jensen

headlines.title: Elderly couple accused of killing son-in-law in Dublin plead not guilty
headlines.description: An elderly couple accused in the killing of their son-in-law in Dublin last month pleaded not guilty Monday to charges of first-degree murder with special circumstances of lying in wait. Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang allegedly both shot their son-in-law, 40-year-old Jonathan McKinsey, to death on Sept. 26 in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin. Curtis Briggs, an attorney for Chen, said McKinsey was at the complex for a supervised visit with his children, who he shared with his estranged wife Candice Jang. Briggs claims Chen and Zhang did not premeditate the alleged crime but rather saw something that made them concerned about the safety of their grandchildren and forced them to act. Briggs did not elaborate. “They are not cold-blooded killers,” Briggs said. “They didn’t premeditate anything. There was nothing planned. They were just concerned grandparents who were afraid for their grandchildren’s safety.” Briggs described the couple as sweet, docile and loving grandparents. He said Chen was a live-in nanny who was devoted to her grandchildren. McKinsey, a gaming engineer for The New York Times, and Jang were in the midst of a bitter divorce and child custody dispute, both accusing the other of physical and emotional abuse. Briggs said McKinsey allegedly threatened to kill Chen at least three times, including once with a hitman. Investigators said Chen had a gun on her when she was arrested. They said they found a second gun in the couple’s car. Briggs said the couple purchased the guns in March for their own protection against McKinsey. A bail hearing was set for Nov. 4, followed by a pre-trial hearing on Nov. 23. Dublin Oct 1 Dublin Sep 30 Couple accused of lying in wait before killing son-in-law at Dublin park

headlines.title: Testimony continues in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Testimony in the corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao resumed Monday with some of the people closest to her taking the stand. Thao is on trial on allegations she offered future contracts with a waste recycling company in exchange that the men behind that company help her get elected mayor. Monday marked the second day of testimony in the trial. Defense attorneys continued their cross-examination of Thao’s former chief of staff, Leigh Hanson. Some of the questioning of Hanson centered around a trip Thao took to Vietnam in 2023, soon after taking office. Hanson said Thao believed the Port of Oakland covered her expenses, but prosecutors argued the majority of that trip was covered by co-defendants, David and Andy Duong, who own California Waste Solutions, which is Oakland’s recycling contractor. Hanson said she had tried to dissuade Thao from taking the trip because of the bad optics of a new mayor traveling to Asia while the city was facing serious budget issues. Sheng Thao Oct 15 Sheng Thao Oct 14 Sheng Thao Oct 13 Hanson on Monday reiterated Thao was angry with Andy Duong after questions arose about alleged sex trafficking of minors on the trip. Hanson testified Thao said Duong had “ruined her career.” Duong’s attorney has disputed the allegations, calling them rumors. During cross-examination last week, Hanson testified that Thao did not intervene to put people in power who prosecutors allege had been backed by the Duongs. Another key witness turned to a different issue: Negative campaign mailers sent weeks before the election. Former Thao campaign consultant, Noah Finneburgh, testified he believed the mailers were racist and drafted a statement condemning them, but the Thao campaign instead approved a tweet response. Finneburgh also testified Thao never said she supported the mailers. Prosecutors claim the mailers were funded and managed by the Duongs and other coconspirators at Thao’s direction. The defense denies that and said Thao and her political adviser and partner at the time, Andre Jones, opposed the mailers. Other revealing details include FBI Special Agent Katherine Barclay testified the entire corruption investigation began after a company hired by Mario Juarez, Evolutionary Homes cofounder, accused him of failing to pay the full cost for the mailers. In court, jurors saw Juarez’s notes and texts, including promises from the Duongs to help Thao in exchange for city contract considerations for their companies, California Waste Solutions and Evolutionary Homes. “No matter what happens in this trial, we know that the people who enable Sheng Thao’s corruption are still running the city of Oakland today,” said Seneca Scott with Oakland Watch. Meanwhile, during a scheduled news conference outside federal court Monday, the leaders behind the recall effort of Thao asked for the end of no-bid contracts, greater transparency and accountability at city hall. The group also campaigned against an upcoming ballot measure that would create a so-called strong-mayor model in Oakland. Thao, Jones and the Duongs have been indicted on charges of bribery, conspiracy and wire fraud. They have all pleaded not guilty. Court resumes Thursday with the FBI special agent’s testimony.
